>40. In modern industrial society only minimal effort is necessary to 
>satisfy one's physical needs. It is enough to go through a training 
>program to acquire some petty technical skill, then come to work on time 
>and exert very modest effort needed to hold a job. The only requirements 
>are a moderate amount of intelligence, and most of all, simple 
>OBEDIENCE. If one has those, society takes care of one from cradle to 
>grave. 

The surrogate activities section has intrigued me ever since I read it. Now, in
part, I know why. I was suffering from severe burnout, due to a manager (who
doesn't work there any more) who took great pleasure in suppressing my
creativity and putting my skills down. OBEDIANCE was paramount to her. She got
laid off, I moved up, and love my new job! Nah na na nah na!  :-) And in French
I would say <<bisque bisque rage!>>:)   I work with some really cool people,
laid back, quite bright, and a few of them would feel right at home on this
newsgroup.

But, I believe that many people aren't as lucky as I am. I saw a study a while
back, and I can't remember the exact statistics, but it seemed that a
significant percentage of people didn't like their jobs, which is a true shame,
since given society's structure, one *has to* work, and spend most of one's
waking hours at it. Sure, one has a choice.  I know that I wouldn't do well in
a cardboard box living in the street. Yet, most people are also only a few
paychecks away from homelessness. What a "system!"

>39. We use the term "surrogate activity" to designate an activity that 
>is directed toward an artificial goal that people set up for themselves 
>merely in order to have some goal to work toward, or let us say, merely 
>for the sake of the "fulfillment" that they get from pursuing the goal. 
>Here is a rule of thumb for the identification of surrogate activities. 
>Given a person who devotes much time and energy to the pursuit of goal 
>X, ask yourself this: If he had to devote most of his time and energy to 
>satisfying his biological needs, and if that effort required him to use 
>his physical and mental facilities in a varied and interesting way, 
>would he feel seriously deprived because he did not attain goal X? If 
>the answer is no, then the person's pursuit of a goal X is a surrogate 
>activity. 

I was always curious about this passage. People have tended to emphasize the
part about  using one's *physical* attributes, while ignoring the remark about
*mental* attributes.

It seemed to me that if one works to fulfill biological needs, including food,
shelter and even "romance" (hey, Happy Hours, etc. can be fun:) and if they
were accomplished using one's mental facilities in a varied and interesting
way, that they are not surrogate activities.

So, I do wish that Ted would elaborate on this concept, because I think it is
truly important. I like my job because it is mentally stimulating, and I work
with great people.  I also occassionally get to crawl around under desks
looking at cabling connections, which might be construed as physical activity,
although I wouldn't go so far:-) But, though I enjoy my job, and it isn't
harmful to anyone, I sometimes wonder about the uselessness of much of what is
done. While I am greatly enjoying the experience of learning so many new
things, this question is always there for me. I think that this is what Ted was
addressing here.

I think it would be really great if we could take our collective knowledge and
use it for something really valuable. But, of course, before we can attempt to
do that, we need to decide what would be valuable. And to decide what valuable
implies.

-Susan
